title: How the hyperparameters were chosen
lead: A game program has dozens of settings that no formula derives. This page shows how this project set them: first how a single result is measured, then seven levels from simple to complex, each with a real example and its measured effect. It ends with what was never tuned.
sec.what.title: What a hyperparameter is
sec.what.p1: A {term:hyperparameter} is a setting that training or search does not learn by itself. The network learns its about {n:62000} {term:weight|weights} from data. Someone still has to choose the {term:learning-rate|learning rate} of that training, the exploration constant `c` of {term:mcts|MCTS} and the {term:node-budget|node budget} of the classical search. In Java terms: the weights are the state an object builds up while it runs; the hyperparameters are its constructor arguments.
sec.what.p2: Every value on this page carries one of two labels. Measured means that an experiment in the repository settled it, with fixed {term:seed|seeds} and an interval. Project decision means that someone chose it and no experiment shows that it is best. Both labels are honest. The second one also tells you where a later experiment could still find strength.
sec.measuring.title: How a result is measured
sec.measuring.p1: Strength is measured with {term:paired-games|paired games}: each opening of 4 random {term:ply|plies} is played twice, with the sides swapped. This removes most of the first-move advantage and of the opening luck. {src:search/src/main/java/sternhalma/search/Arena.java} plays the pairs and reports the mean score; a win counts 1, a loss 0. Every strength run fixes a {term:node-limit|node or simulation count} instead of a time limit, so the result does not depend on how busy the machine is. A candidate that is slower per node plays at {term:equal-cost|equal cost} and gets correspondingly fewer nodes.
sec.measuring.p2: The score becomes an {term:elo|Elo} difference, `400 · log10(s / (1 − s))` ({src:search/src/main/java/sternhalma/search/Elo.java}); a score of {n:0.64} is about +100 Elo. Each result comes with a 95 % {term:confidence-interval|confidence interval} from the {term:standard-error|standard error} of the pair scores. Near a score of 1 the curve gets steep, and above about {n:0.85} a match resolves nothing: the opponent is {term:saturation|saturated}. Loop run 4 scored {n:0.82} to {n:0.91} against the classical ladder and showed no gain there, while a direct match showed +78 ± 19 Elo.
sec.measuring.p3: The {term:seed|seeds} of the random openings are split by role: authors tune on seeds 31 and 32, report on 33 and 34, and a verifier re-measures on 41 and 42. This is the same idea as keeping test data out of the training set: a value tuned on the report seeds would partly fit their luck. For quick tuning loops the arena can stop early with an {term:sprt|SPRT} ({src:search/src/main/java/sternhalma/search/Sprt.java}); verifier runs always play a fixed number of pairs.
sec.decisions.title: Level 0: chosen, not varied
sec.decisions.p1: The simplest way to set a value is to choose it. Many values in this project were chosen once and never varied. Examples are the {term:adamw|AdamW} betas {n:0.9} and {n:0.999}, epsilon `1e-8` and {term:weight-decay|weight decay} {n:0.01} ({src:nn/src/main/java/sternhalma/nn/Optimizer.java}), and the training {term:batch} of 256 samples. The {term:dirichlet-noise|Dirichlet noise} of self-play, with alpha {n:0.3} and weight {n:0.25}, follows common AlphaZero practice ({src:selfplay/src/main/java/sternhalma/selfplay/LoopConfig.java}). The training documents label several of them "proposal, to measure" ({src:docs/training.md}).
sec.decisions.p2: The five strength levels of the app are node budgets: {n:1000}, {n:5000}, {n:20000}, {n:100000} and {n:500000} ({src:web/src/ui/Panels.tsx}). A procedure to calibrate them as an Elo ladder is written down ({src:docs/search-and-evaluation.md}), but no result exists, so the levels are a project decision. The same holds for the {n:20000} nodes of every reference player: the number appears in the earliest experiments, and nobody recorded why it was chosen.
sec.hand-tuning.title: Level 1: tuned by hand
sec.hand-tuning.p1: The first correction to the distance evaluation, `stage4`, has four weights: straggler (`ws`), squared distance (`wq`), cohesion (`wc`) and jump bridges (`wj`, forward jumps that are possible now). The search documents call them free parameters that only tournament tuning can set ({src:docs/search-and-evaluation.md}). They were tuned by hand in the arena at {n:5000} nodes on seeds 3 and 4, then measured at {n:20000} nodes on seeds 1 and 2, with 200 pairs each; these early runs predate the split of seeds by role. The result was `ws=15`, `wq=6`, `wj=3` and `wc=0`.
sec.hand-tuning.p2: Against the plain distance evaluation, the tuned weights won by +306 ± 41 and +371 ± 51 Elo. Cohesion was the surprise: `wc=5` lost by more than 450 Elo, and `wc=±1` changed nothing. The documents record these results, but not which other values were tried. The outcome can be checked; the search that led to it cannot be repeated.
sec.regression.title: Level 2: fitted by regression
sec.regression.p1: The project then replaced hand tuning by a fit. The learned linear {term:evaluation-function|evaluation} uses {term:logistic-regression|logistic regression}: it predicts the game result from the {term:feature|features} of a position, and the fitted weights become the evaluation. The first fit had 12 weights and used about {n:68000} positions from {n:2000} games. A later refit added a 13th feature, the best one-move distance gain; that gives the 13 weights of {sec:classical/evaluation|topic 2}. Chess programmers call this {term:texel-tuning|Texel tuning}. The weights are in {src:search/src/main/java/sternhalma/search/LinearWeights.java}.
sec.regression.p2: On 400 {term:held-out-set|held-out} games the fit predicts the winner of {n:78.8} % of positions; the distance difference alone predicts {n:76.8} %. In the arena the fitted evaluation won by +552 ± 89 and +577 ± 96 Elo at equal nodes. The regression supplied the weights, and the tournament decided whether to keep them.
sec.regression.p3: The lesson came with the second fit. It predicted the results better but played weaker (seed 4: +440 against +526 Elo), so the first weights stayed. A later refit showed the same pattern: a fit without race positions gained about twice as much as a fit with them, although the fit with them had the lower held-out {term:log-loss|log loss}. A better fit to the data does not make a better player. Later refits also had to beat a different evaluator family, which catches {term:overfitting} to self-play.
sec.grids.title: Level 3: small grids
sec.grids.p1: A {term:grid-search|grid search} tries every combination of a few values. The alpha-beta search has options such as {term:principal-variation-search|principal variation search}, {term:killer-move|killer moves} and {term:late-move-reductions|late move reductions} (LMR). Each was tried on seeds 3 and 4 with 200 pairs against the baseline at {n:20000} nodes. All options together with `lmr=2` won: +212 ± 38 and +180 ± 37, re-measured on seeds 1 and 2 at +175 and +143. At {n:20000} nodes, depth 4 costs about {n:9000} nodes and depth 5 about {n:85000}; LMR turns wasted nodes into depth ({src:search/src/main/java/sternhalma/search/Strategies.java}).
sec.grids.p2: The {term:futility-pruning|futility} margins came from a measurement plus a grid. First a probe over about {n:129000} moves measured how far a move's value exceeds the quick estimate `static + 30 × gain`; that gives a safe margin. Then 14 margin settings played on the tuning seeds 31 and 32. The arena chose small margins, `fut=1`, `futk=30`, `fut2=1`. On the report seeds 33 and 34 they won +139 ± 27 and +142 ± 28 Elo at equal cost: a cut that is sometimes wrong costs less than the extra depth gains.
sec.grids.p3: A grid can also be judged by a statistical bound instead of a tournament. {term:adjudication|Adjudication} ends a game early when the result is clear. Its score margin of 500 over two own moves came from an offline sweep over 400 and 500 and over one and two moves. The margin was accepted because it was wrong once in 993 firings: the {term:clopper-pearson|Clopper-Pearson} upper bound on its error rate is {n:0.477} %.
sec.sweeps.title: Level 4: one-dimensional sweeps
sec.sweeps.p1: A sweep varies one value and keeps everything else fixed. The {term:mcts|MCTS} settings of the network engine were swept this way on one seed: the exploration constant `c` of {term:puct|PUCT}, the leaf {term:batch} size and the prior temperature ({sec:inference/mcts|how MCTS uses `c`}). Each setting played with 100 {term:simulation|simulations} per move against the best classical player at 400 and then {n:1600} nodes.
sec.sweeps.p2: At batch 1, `c` = {n:0.5} gave +252 Elo, {n:1.0} gave +338 ± 70, {n:1.5} gave +269, {n:2.5} gave +108 and {n:4.0} gave +33. At `c` = {n:0.5}, batch 1 gave +542 ± 136, batch 4 +478, batch 16 +323 and batch 64 +85: larger batches need {term:virtual-loss|virtual loss}, which costs strength, and the CPU forward pass gains nothing from batching. Prior temperature {n:1.0} was best. The defaults are in {src:search/src/main/java/sternhalma/search/MctsOptions.java}.
sec.sweeps.p3: The training documents add an honest caveat ({src:docs/training.md}): the curve is flat within the noise between `c` = {n:0.5} and {n:1.5}, so choosing {n:1.0} over {n:0.5} is not supported by a significant difference. A fresh seed even reversed the order: {n:0.5} gave +372 ± 83, {n:1.0} gave +272 ± 66. A sweep on one seed finds the flat region; it cannot pick a winner inside it.
sec.recipe-sweep.title: Level 5: the training recipe sweep
sec.recipe-sweep.p1: Loop run 2 of the training rejected three generations in a row (gate scores {n:0.509}, {n:0.491} and {n:0.496}) with a constant learning rate of `3e-4`. Sweep 1 searched for the cause offline: 8 training recipes, each trained from the same start network on the same set of about {n:588000} samples, with the same batches in the same order. Only the learning-rate schedule, the number of steps or the value weight differed. A baseline recipe first reproduced the loop's candidate bit for bit, which proved that the tool was faithful ({src:selfplay/src/main/java/sternhalma/selfplay/Sweep.java}).
sec.recipe-sweep.p2: Each recipe played the loop's {term:gate} of 200 pairs against the start network. The winner, variant F, was a {term:cosine-decay|cosine decay} from `3e-4` to `1e-5` over {n:15000} steps, with a gate score of {n:0.5625} (standard error {n:0.0184}). The same {n:15000} steps at a constant rate scored {n:0.481}, so more steps made it worse. The constant learning rate was the problem ({sec:training/learning|learning rate and schedule}). Loop run 3 used the new recipe and left the stall behind.
sec.recipe-sweep.p3: Picking the best of eight noisy gate scores overestimates the winner; this is {term:selection-bias|selection bias}. Variant F was therefore confirmed on 400 fresh pairs: {n:0.5887} (standard error {n:0.0136}), about +62 Elo. The training documents also name the limits ({src:docs/training.md}): one start point, one data set, one training seed. The cheap held-out numbers such as the {term:kl-divergence|KL divergence} hardly told the recipes apart, so the gate stayed the criterion.
sec.pre-registered.title: Level 6: rules fixed in advance
sec.pre-registered.p1: The last level fixes the decision rule before the experiment runs ({term:pre-registration|pre-registration}), so a result cannot quietly move the goal. The capacity test trained four network sizes from scratch on the same data ({src:selfplay/src/main/java/sternhalma/selfplay/Capacity.java}). The rule set in advance: a larger network goes into the loop only if its held-out KL is at least {n:0.03} lower and it wins the gate with at least {n:0.58}. After {n:128000} steps the LARGE network beat the best network of loop run 3 with {n:0.688}, about +138 Elo.
sec.pre-registered.p2: The number of simulations in training followed a threshold of +80 Elo per doubling, fixed before the measurement. The measurement gave about +110 Elo per doubling, so the next loops used 800 simulations instead of 200. The stop rule was fixed the same way: if after two generations no confirmed candidate beat generation 11 of loop run 4 by at least {n:0.55} over 400 pairs, training would end. None did, so training ended after loop run 7.
sec.pre-registered.p3: The gate's promotion rule is the same idea in code: a candidate replaces the best network only if `score − 1.28 · se > 0.5` ({src:selfplay/src/main/java/sternhalma/selfplay/Gate.java}). Loop run 1 had used `score > 0.5`, which promotes half of all candidates that are merely equal; with {term:z-score|z} = {n:1.28} that happens in 10 % of gates. The rule also shows its own resolution: with the gate's 200 pairs, a true gain of +16 Elo passes only about half of the gates.
sec.never-tuned.title: What was never tuned
sec.never-tuned.p1: Some values were never tuned. The AdamW betas, epsilon and weight decay were never varied. Batch size and weight decay are listed under "not tried" in {src:docs/training.md}, and the {term:reuse-factor|reuse factor} of the training samples is still unmeasured. The teacher temperature of generation 0 was measured, with an optimum of {n:0.06} at depth 3 and {n:0.05} at depth 2, but the defaults {n:0.1} and {n:0.06} stayed. Loop run 4 used the learning rate `1e-4` instead of the `3e-4` that sweep 1 favoured, and the reason was not found.
sec.never-tuned.p2: No automated tuner was used anywhere: no {term:random-search|random search}, no {term:bayesian-optimisation|Bayesian optimisation} and no {term:spsa|SPSA}. Every sweep was a small grid that a person chose and a tournament judged. The reading list below covers these methods and the statistics behind the intervals. Every term from all six topics is collected in the {sec:glossary/hyperparameter|glossary}.
